newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Gold slips to lowest fixing since April,'94.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Gold slips to lowest fixing since April,'94.

text.p: Gold prices continued to slide on Thursday on a combination of speculators getting out of loss-making positions and selling by Australian and South African producers.
Gold fixed in London at $372.20 per ounce, the lowest since April 25, 1994, and down from $373.00 on Wednesday
The April 25, 1994 fixing was $370.25 and there were few players around willing to bet that that would not be beaten in the near future.
"A hefty fall in the Dow, or the dollar coming off will be needed to get some interest in gold again," one dealer said.
Dealers said the market had been losing ground all week as the professionals squared off their positions ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday which shuts most U.S. markets until Monday.
"It could be quite thin until then but if somebody tries a move, the lack of market participants will exaggerate it," one dealer said.
Market confidence has been seriously shaken recently by a series of factors all of which have been interpreted as potentially damaging for gold.
"Almost everything that could go wrong for it, has gone wrong," one analyst said.
One source of nervousness was rumours that the European central banks could sell gold from their reserves to meet European Monetary Union convergence criteria.
Then the International Monetary Fund confirmed that it would sell five million ounces from its gold reserve if it failed to raise funds to help the world's poorest nations by other means.

Next a director of the ultra gold-conservative Swiss National Bank voiced the opinion that Switzerland should reduce the level of gold backing for its currency from 40 percent and opening the possibility of selling or lending formerly inactive gold reserves.
Analysts estimate the central banks and other institutions hold over 35,000 tonnes of gold in their reserves, the vast majority of which is inactive and kept well away from the market

Adding to the anxiety was news that the Russian Finance Ministry will take over sales of domestic gold output, which was interpretted as meaning Russia would be a more willing exporter of gold and precious stones.
"These structural movements in thinking have made the market nervous and rightly so," one analyst said.
"The investment funds which have the fleetest feet of all have done the right thing and got out," he added.

But another sign of the lack of confidence in gold has been reported selling of metal by gold miners from South Africa and Australia where, due to strengthening local currencies, domestic gold prices have been falling even faster than on the international market.
"The producers seem to have decided this is not just a blip but that the price will continue to fall," said bullion analyst Andy Smith of Union Bank of Switzerland.
"Otherwise they would be taking advantage of these low prices to buy gold to sell back into the market at high prices later," he added.
Smith forecast that the gold price's next move would be decided when the New York markets return from holiday on Monday.
The other precious metals were also struggling at lower levels on Thursday.
Platinum and palladium prices weakened after Japanese Finance Ministry data showed imports in October were down by 28.8 and 26.9 percent respectively against October 1995.
Platinum fixed at $374.25 an ounce, the lowest fixing since December 6, 1993 and palladium fixed at $114.25 an ounce, the lowest since April 16, 1993.
Silver prices were relatively unscathed, shedding only a cent overnight to $4.72/$4.74.
